vignette:
He is a 34-year-old publisher, married for seven years to a woman he met in graduate school. They have no children yet. He arrives to each session punctually, dressed in pressed shirts and tailored blazers, but there is a tightness in his jaw that never fully releases. He speaks in measured sentences, often stopping mid-thought to check that his wife is safe—he texts her during sessions, phone face-down on the armrest.

Two years ago, he was at a literary fair in another city, signing contracts for a debut novel by a young refugee writer. The afternoon was bright, full of handshakes and book stacks. Then his phone buzzed: a number he did not recognize, a voice he did not believe. His wife, driving home from her own job, had been T-boned at an intersection by a driver who ran a red light. The caller was a trauma nurse who kept saying stable but critical like a mantra. He chartered a small plane. He remembers the way the clouds looked—thin, broken, like torn pages.

His wife survived. Three surgeries, four months of rehabilitation, a scar that runs from her collarbone to her waist. But something in him did not survive whole. He has not driven on that particular highway since the day of the accident. He takes back streets, even if it adds forty minutes to his commute. The noise of a hard brake makes his hands shake. He cannot watch any movie or television show that includes a car crash. Last month, a trailer for a thriller played before a film he and his wife were watching in their living room. He stood up, walked to the bedroom, and sat on the edge of the bed until his breathing slowed.

At work, he is the publisher of a modest independent press that focuses on immigrant voices. He used to love reading slush pile submissions late into the night. Now he cannot finish a manuscript that contains even a hint of sudden loss. He tells his assistant to screen for "high emotional content" without being able to explain what he means. Two promising novels about war and displacement are sitting in his inbox, unread. He avoids the authors' emails. He cancels meetings last minute. His business partner has started to ask if he is okay. He says he is fine.

He is not fine.

At night, he wakes with his heart pounding. He sees the accident not as a memory but as a scene he is living again: the phone call, the nurse's voice, the helplessness of being six hundred miles away. He checks his wife's breathing, feels her pulse, watches the rise and fall of her chest until his own lungs feel heavy. She tells him he is smothering her. He knows this. He cannot stop. She started seeing her own therapist six months ago. That was when he finally made the call to schedule an intake for himself.

In the waiting room before sessions, he sometimes scrolls through old photos on his phone—before the crash, when her smile was effortless and his own shoulders were loose. He does not believe she will ever be truly safe again. The world, to him, has become a series of unforseen catastrophes waiting to happen. The sentence he wrote on his intake questionnaire, under most distressing event, was: "I wasn't there."

He is here now, in the chair, looking at the therapist with the same controlled expression he uses in contract negotiations. He says he wants to sleep through a night. He says he wants to stop feeling like a man standing on a high ledge. He says he wants to read a book again and remember what it felt like to be moved instead of terrified. His hands are folded. The clock on the wall ticks. Outside, traffic hums, and he flinches at the sound of a horn.
